In a workplace, there may be circumstances when you have to explain your intention for doing something or to talk about certain requirements of the job.

You use purpose clauses to introduce your intentions or to talk about requirements.
The most common way to express purpose is to use a to-infinitive (called an infinitive of purpose). You use this to emphasize one specific purpose.

I phoned to find out when the project is due.
I didn't do it to take the credit away from you.
Two common phrases to express purpose or intention are: in order to and so as to.

I arrived early so as to appear motivated.
I prepared yesterday in order to feel confident today.
I wanted you to come see me in order to discuss the internal job posting you applied for.
In order to help you, I'll be sending you an email with everything you need to know.
I have a few questions actually so as to get a better understanding of the position.
You use the Future Continuous tense to talk about something happening at a particular time in the future and to create a sense of atmosphere about the future.
The action will have started before that moment but it will not have finished at that moment.
I will be working at the office next week.
The person will start work at some point in the future and be working next week. It is not clear when the person will stop working.
There are two ways to use the Future Continuous tense:
1. You use the Future Continuous to indicate that a longer action in the future will be interrupted by a shorter action in the future.
I will be waiting for you when your bus arrives.
Notice that the interruption (arrives) is in the Simple Present tense. You cannot use future tenses in time clauses (when, while, before, after, by the time, as soon as, if, unless).
2. You use the Future Continuous to express the idea that two actions will be happening at the same time. The actions are parallel. You use two Future Continuous actions in the same sentence.
I am going to be writing and he is going to be checking facts.
The structure of the Future Continuous is:
I'll be sending you an email with everything you need to know.
Will I be taking part in more meetings now?
You'll also be undertaking more responsibilities and working longer hours.

When you add -ing or -ed to verbs ending in e, like receive, you remove the e.

Denise: Kristi, can you pop by my office when you have a moment?
Kristi: Sure.
Denise: Please, have a seat. I wanted you to come see me in order to discuss the internal job posting you applied for.
Kristi: Great, I was actually going to come see you at the end of the day in regards to that.
Denise: Well then, let's get down to business. After much consideration, we have decided to go with you. You've been promoted!
Kristi: Ah, really? Wow, thank you! Thanks so much!
Denise: No problem. You'll be starting as a junior editor on Tuesday.

Kristi: So quickly? Will I be ready?
Denise: Of course. In order to help you, I'll be sending you an email with everything you need to know.
Kristi: Will I be taking part in more meetings now?
Denise: Yes. You'll also be undertaking more responsibilities and working longer hours.
Kristi: I have a few questions actually so as to get a better understanding of the position.
Denise: Alright.
Kristi: Will I being getting paid for overtime?
Denise: Not necessarily. Instead of being paid, the extra hours will be used as time off in lieu. Essentially, you'll be banking hours. You will be receiving a salary increase as mentioned in your interview.

Kristi: What about a benefit plan?
Denise: As you know, you qualify for benefits with the company after three months of employment.
Kristi: Here's where I would like some clarification. For me to qualify for benefits, do I need to wait another three months?
Denise: Ah, no. You've already been with us for over a month. So, just another two to go.
Kristi: Okay, that's good to know. Another question I had which was briefly touched upon in my interview is about traveling for this job.
Denise: Yes, there may be times you'll be traveling. Keep in mind that these trips are usually within the country, not overseas. And of course, all travel expenses are covered by us. You may be traveling sometime soon, Kristi. BFP Publishing has a lot of plans for the future.
